blocks.text: A catalytic converter is a ceramic or metallic monolith with a honeycomb-like structure (Figure 12.6). Its inner channels carry a layer of alumina to provide a high surface area, and the expensive noble metals platinum, palladium and rhodium are dispersed on the alumina. These metals catalyse three redox reactions that remove the harmful exhaust gases: the three-way converter converts harmful CO, NO and hydrocarbons into CO2, N2 and water. The precious metals can be recycled. Reduction: 2NO(g) + 2CO(g) over Pt/Rd gives N2(g) + 2CO2(g). Oxidation: 2CO(g) + O2(g) over Pt/Rh gives 2CO2(g), and 2C2H4 + 6O2 over Pt/Rd gives 4CO2 + 4H2O.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: 'Rd' is not an element symbol; the catalyst is platinum/rhodium, Pt/Rh, as the book writes for the CO oxidation.

blocks.alt: Cut-away view of a catalytic converter: an outlet pipe on the left, a wider metal body holding two honeycomb monolith blocks, and an inlet pipe on the right. Thick yellow arrows show HC, CO, NOx entering at the lower right, passing through the honeycomb and leaving at the upper left as H2O, CO2, N2. A leader line points into a block with the label 'washcoat with catalyst inside the monolith channel'.
